content: 1. Once the woman is clinically stable, administer ferrous sulfate, folic acid, and multivitamins to support her nutritional needs. 2. If possible, adhere to Ministry of Health (MoH) or World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for HIV testing and prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. 3. Provide antibiotic prophylaxis for ruptured membranes and consider it for cases of incomplete abortion, obstetric hemorrhage, or retained placenta. 4. Administer antibiotics if there is suspicion of chorioamnionitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, or tubo-ovarian abscess. Antibiotics may also be considered for intrauterine procedures or after normal spontaneous vaginal delivery if there is concern for secondary infection. 5. Pre-assembled delivery kits containing essential items such as plastic umbilical cord clamps, gauze, disposable scissors, absorbent drapes, menstrual pads, highly absorbent pads, and misoprostol for postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) prevention should be readily available in all health facilities, including those in Ebola and non-Ebola settings, to reduce childbirth risks. 6. Pre-assembled kits should also be available for managing obstetric complications like PPH and eclampsia. 7. Surgical management of complications such as obstructed labor depends on the expertise and capacity of the Ebola Treatment Unit (ETU) staff, with careful attention to risks and adherence to infection prevention and control (IPC) measures. Management of Suspected and Confirmed Ebola Patients 8. Minimize health worker exposure to blood and bodily fluids during procedures by organizing a team of four trained staff, including two experienced in childbirth and emergency obstetric care, a cleaner for decontamination, and an observer to ensure IPC safety. 9. Use full personal protective equipment (PPE) for childbirth care in Ebola settings, including head cover, face mask, goggles or face shield, boots, coverall or gown, apron, and double gloves with outer elbow-length gloves. 10. Strictly maintain IPC standards, including handwashing, safe disposal of waste contaminated with blood or bodily fluids, proper handling of soiled linen, careful handling and disposal of sharps, and disinfection of instruments and equipment. 11. Avoid the use of sharp instruments where possible; disposable scissors are an option. 12. Limit vaginal examinations and invasive procedures during labor and childbirth. 13. Wear full PPE during childbirth care, changing the outer gloves and washing gloved hands between procedures. 14. Place a peripheral IV early to facilitate venous access for emergency IV fluid or medication administration. 15. Allow spontaneous labor without interruption. Do not perform artificial rupture of membranes and limit vaginal examinations. Use a partograph if feasible. 16. Measure fetal heart rate with a Doppler on admission to the Ebola treatment facility and as clinically indicated. Continuous fetal monitoring is not advised. 17. Administer a uterotonic drug immediately after delivery to prevent PPH, following WHO and national guidelines. If a skilled birth attendant is unavailable, administer misoprostol and wait for placental expulsion. 18. If the baby is stillborn, there is no need to clamp and cut the cord. If the baby is born alive, wait one to three minutes after birth or until the cord stops pulsating, then clamp the cord with two disposable clamps and cut it with disposable scissors. 19. Carefully consider health worker safety and clinical outcomes before performing invasive procedures such as episiotomy, manual removal of the placenta, or vacuum extraction. Limit exposure to sharps and excess fluids by considering safer alternative treatment approaches, such as applying external pressure with absorbent pads to superficial perineal lacerations instead of immediate suture repair. 20. If the woman is clinically stable, manage retained placenta conservatively with uterotonic agents and extended observation before considering manual removal. Only trained providers with elbow-length gloves should perform manual removal of the placenta. 21. Upon discharge from the ETU, provide counseling on breastfeeding, prevention of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and family planning methods. Prevention of Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) 22. Ensure there is no second baby in the uterus before administering uterotonic drugs. 23. Oxytocin is the uterotonic drug of choice for PPH prevention and treatment. If oxytocin is unavailable or not feasible, use misoprostol. 24. Administer oral misoprostol 600 μg immediately after the final baby is born for PPH prevention. If the patient cannot take oral medication, administer 400 μg sublingually. 25. If an IV infusion is in place, administer oxytocin IV 10 IU as a slow push using a three-way connector. Alternatively, IM oxytocin (10 IU) injection may be used, but sharp exposure risks should be considered. Treatment of Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) 26. Oxytocin remains the preferred uterotonic drug. Administer 40 units of oxytocin in 1 liter of IV fluid, initially at 60 drops per minute until the uterus contracts, then reduce the infusion rate to 40 drops per minute. 27. If oxytocin is not feasible, administer misoprostol 800 μg sublingually. 28. Perform external uterine massage with protective covering (e.g., absorbable pads) on the patient’s abdomen while standing to the side to avoid direct exposure to blood and bodily fluids. External aortic compression may also be considered. 29. Consider using a non-pneumatic anti-shock garment as a temporizing measure for obstetric hemorrhage treatment if available and staff are trained in its use. Newborn Care 30. Provide essential newborn care per WHO guidelines, including keeping the baby warm and dry. 31. Administer Vitamin K intramuscularly, and if possible, provide routine immunizations such as BCG and hepatitis B. 32. Take appropriate infection prevention measures to avoid neonatal infection through cord care. 33. Ensure neonatal resuscitation equipment (e.g., suction, bag, and mask) and trained providers are available. 34. Actively manage neonates with confirmed Ebola in the ETU, including supportive care and antibiotic coverage for possible neonatal sepsis. Induction of Labor at Term 35. Do not use misoprostol for induction if the patient has a history of previous cesarean delivery or uterine surgery. 36. As gestational size increases, the uterus becomes more sensitive to misoprostol, so lower doses should be used. 37. Administer misoprostol 20–25 μg orally every two hours. If using 200 μg tablets, dissolve in 200 ml of water and give 20 ml every two hours. Treatment of Incomplete Abortion/Miscarriage 38. Pregnant patients with Ebola are at increased risk for spontaneous abortion. Minimize health worker exposure to blood and bodily fluids. 39. Use misoprostol for treating incomplete abortion to avoid needle use and other instrumental procedures. 40. For uterine size equivalent to ≤13 weeks gestation, provide a single dose of misoprostol 400 μg sublingually. 41. For uterine size >13 weeks gestation, administer misoprostol 400 μg sublingually, repeating every 3–4 hours if necessary. 42. If bleeding is excessive and the woman’s condition deteriorates, provide IV fluids (e.g., Lactated Ringer’s) or blood transfusion with fresh whole blood, and consider manual vacuum aspiration with safety precautions. Post-Abortion Care 43. Provide appropriate post-abortion care, including contraceptive counseling and methods of post-abortion contraception, such as emergency contraception. 44. Promote dual protection (e.g., condoms alone or with another method) to prevent both pregnancy and STIs. 45. Advise women to use contraception for at least six months to reduce risks of adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes. Pregnant Women in the ETU Who Become PCR-Negative 46. Determine fetal viability using Doppler or ultrasound. If fetal demise is confirmed, consider induction of labor with careful planning, counseling, and consent. 47. If the fetus is viable, counsel the woman on potential fetal outcomes based on current evidence. 48. Treat all pregnancy-associated tissues and fluids as potentially infectious, and health workers should use full PPE plus elbow-length gynecologic gloves. 49. Provide accurate information and counseling to enable informed decision-making regarding pregnancy continuation or termination. Management of Newborns with Elevated Risk of Ebola 50. Monitor asymptomatic neonates closely for 21 days in an Ebola care facility using full PPE and IPC precautions. 51. Obtain samples of amniotic fluid, neonatal oral and surface swabs, and cord blood for Ebola PCR testing at delivery. 52. Test asymptomatic neonates on days 22 and 24, and discharge them only if both tests are negative.
